title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: Every graph on $n$ vertices admits a strongly-separating path system of size $O(n)$.
context_text: The weakly-separating version of this conjecture was independently posed by Falgas-Ravry, Kittipassorn, Korándi, Letzter, and Narayanan (2014), and later strengthened to strongly-separating path systems by Balogh, Csaba, Martin, and Pluhár (2016). Letzter had previously made major progress by proving an $O(n \log^\star n)$ bound. The question originates from G.O.H. Katona (2013) in the tradition of separating systems initiated by Rényi in 1961.
attributed_to: Balogh, Csaba, Martin, and Pluhár; Falgas-Ravry, Kittipassorn, Korándi, Letzter, and Narayanan
paper_contribution: Confirms the conjecture by proving that every graph on $n$ vertices admits a strongly-separating path system of size $19n$.
paper_title: Separating the edges of a graph by a linear number of paths

title: Problem 3
statement_text: Does every graph on $n$ vertices admit a strongly-separating path system of size $2n$?
context_text: A path separates an edge $e$ from an edge $f$ if it contains $e$ but not $f$. A collection $\mathcal{P}$ of paths of $G$ is a strongly-separating path system if for any two distinct edges $e,f$ there are paths $P_e,P_f\in\mathcal{P}$ with $e\in P_e$, $f\notin P_e$, $f\in P_f$, $e\notin P_f$ (weakly-separating if some path contains exactly one of $e,f$); its size is the number of paths. The question, due to Katona, is how many paths are needed; Falgas-Ravry, Kittipassorn, Korándi, Letzter and Narayanan (weak version) and Balogh, Csaba, Martin and Pluhár (strong version) conjectured that $O(n)$ paths always suffice for $n$-vertex graphs, and Letzter proved $O(n\log^\star n)$. The paper confirms the conjecture: every graph on $n$ vertices admits a strongly-separating path system of size $19n$ (using Pósa rotation–extension to reduce to graphs with a Hamiltonian path). This bound is likely far from optimal: Balogh et al. showed that $K_{\varepsilon n,(1-\varepsilon)n}$ cannot be strongly separated by fewer than $2(1-2\varepsilon)n$ paths, and no graph with a larger lower bound is known, suggesting that $2n$ might suffice. Determining the exact constant is challenging even for cliques.
paper_title: Separating the edges of a graph by a linear number of paths

title: Problem 4
statement_text: Does every properly edge-colored graph $G$ admit $O(|V(G)|)$ rainbow paths that cover $E(G)$?
context_text: A proper edge-coloring gives distinct colors to edges sharing an endpoint, and a rainbow path is a path with no two edges of the same color. A path separates an edge $e$ from an edge $f$ if it contains $e$ but not $f$. A collection $\mathcal{P}$ of paths of $G$ is a strongly-separating path system if for any two distinct edges $e,f$ there are paths $P_e,P_f\in\mathcal{P}$ with $e\in P_e$, $f\notin P_e$, $f\in P_f$, $e\notin P_f$ (weakly-separating if some path contains exactly one of $e,f$); its size is the number of paths. The question, due to Katona, is how many paths are needed; Falgas-Ravry, Kittipassorn, Korándi, Letzter and Narayanan (weak version) and Balogh, Csaba, Martin and Pluhár (strong version) conjectured that $O(n)$ paths always suffice for $n$-vertex graphs, and Letzter proved $O(n\log^\star n)$. The paper proves this conjecture, with $19n$ paths. The rainbow question arose in the authors' first attempts and, as far as they know, has not been stated before. An affirmative answer would give another proof of the linear bound: take a path decomposition of $G$ into $O(n)$ paths, split each path into two matchings, form two graphs each containing one matching of each path (the matchings properly color them), and combine rainbow path covers of these two graphs with the original decomposition. The authors can verify the version where paths are replaced by trails.
